**No. Writing all the lyrics does not automatically let you use any free AI-generated song commercially.** Your rights in the lyrics and your permission to use the generated recording are separate.

Assuming the lyrics are original and you own the relevant rights, you can generally authorise their use as an input. That resolves the lyrics question. It does not establish rights to everything the service adds: the melody, arrangement, instrumental performance, generated vocals or final recording.

The key distinctions are:

| Question | What your lyric authorship establishes |
| --- | --- |
| May you supply the lyrics? | Generally yes, assuming you own the relevant rights. |
| May you generate or download a song for free? | Depends on the service’s account and export rules. |
| May you commercially release or use that recording? | Requires permission covering that output and intended use. |
| Do you own enforceable copyright in all generated elements? | Not automatically; this depends on applicable law and human authorship. |

“Free” describes price, not the scope of permission. A service might offer free generation or downloads while limiting outputs to personal or noncommercial use. Another might permit commercial use subject to conditions. Neither possibility can be assumed here because **no account terms or output licence has been supplied**.

Likewise, being able to download a recording establishes technical availability, not commercial clearance. A paid subscription would not settle the question by itself either: the relevant evidence would need to cover the particular output, including any distinctions based on when it was generated or which account tier applied. An upgrade should not be assumed to retroactively change an earlier output’s permissions.

Commercial use also reaches beyond directly selling the song. Using it in a product advertisement, promotional video or business campaign may be commercial even if the video itself earns no advertising revenue. The intended use must fit the permission actually granted.

There is a further distinction between **permission to use** and **copyright ownership**. A provider’s licence may permit commercial exploitation without establishing that you hold exclusive copyright in every generated element. Conversely, owning the lyrics does not override restrictions governing use of the provider’s output. Any relevant third-party material, samples or voice rights would need separate consideration; no such issues have been established for a particular song here.
